subsection: 3. Case study of a developing economy

notes.h: Colonialism: definition and the colonial economy
notes.b: Colonialism is the control of one territory and its people by a foreign power. The colonising country rules the colony (the territory it controls), settles it and/or exploits its resources for its own benefit, and that purpose shaped the colony's economy.
points: Imperialism is the wider policy of building an empire, that is, a group of territories ruled from one centre. Colonialism is how that policy works on the ground in each territory.
The main European colonial powers were Britain, France, Spain, Portugal, the Netherlands, Belgium and Germany.
The Americas were colonised first, then India and Asia, and then Africa, so the periods of colonial rule differ from region to region.

Africa was divided among European powers in the Scramble for Africa after the Berlin Conference (1884–85), which set the rules for European claims. By 1914 only Ethiopia and Liberia in Africa were still independent of European rule.

Colonies supplied cheap raw materials (unprocessed goods) such as cotton, sugar, rubber and minerals to the colonial power, and bought its manufactured goods. This made the colony a supplier and a market rather than a manufacturer.
Local industries that competed with these imports were destroyed, so the colony lost its own manufacturing.
Plantations (large farms growing one crop for sale) and mines used forced or slave labour, which kept the cost of raw materials low.
Food crops were replaced by cash crops (crops grown for sale and export, not for local food), a pattern called monoculture, meaning growing mainly one crop.
notes.tip: A Higher 30-mark question asks you to examine the impact of colonialism on a developing economy you have studied. Name the country, give dates, and cover raw materials, cash crops and destroyed industries.

notes.h: Colonial infrastructure and legacies
notes.b: Colonial powers built transport and institutions to serve their own needs, and independent states inherited the results. The legacy (what was left behind) was economic, political and social.
points: Railways and roads ran from the interior to the ports so that raw materials could be exported. They were not built to link regions with each other, so movement between regions stayed poor.
Ports and capitals grew into the main cities, so development was concentrated on the coast.
Positive legacies are debated: railways, ports, some irrigation, legal and administrative systems, and a world language. Present both sides in an answer.
Most of this infrastructure was built to serve the colonial power rather than the colony's own people, which is why its benefits are debated.
Artificial borders drawn in Europe split some ethnic groups and grouped rival ones together, which created tension inside the new states.
The colonial power's policy of divide and rule (keeping a population weak by setting its groups against one another) set groups against one another.
European languages and religions spread, education reached only a small elite, racial hierarchies (rankings of people by race) were enforced, and land was owned by a few.
Weak institutions (governments, courts and civil services) were handed over at independence, and conflict and coups (seizures of power by the army) followed in many new states.
notes.tip: Examiners expect infrastructure built for export, borders and political legacy, and social legacy. Present the positive legacies as debated, not as simply good.

notes.h: Adjusting to a global economy: general stages
notes.b: After independence, governments tried a sequence of strategies to make their economies work in a world market dominated by rich countries. Each country below follows some of these stages.
points: Import substitution industrialisation: new home industries were protected from foreign competition by tariffs (taxes on imported goods), so local firms could make what had been imported.

Neo-colonialism (new colonialism without direct rule): former colonies often stayed dependent on exporting a few raw materials to rich countries at low and unstable prices, and on foreign loans and companies.

Debt crises in the 1980s and 1990s, when countries could not repay what they owed, led to IMF (International Monetary Fund) and World Bank structural adjustment programmes. These cut government spending, privatised state firms (sold them to private owners), opened markets to trade, and devalued the currency.
Liberalisation: opening the economy to trade and foreign investment, and privatising state firms.
Export diversification: moving beyond a few raw materials into manufactured and service exports, so the country is less exposed to one price.
Joining the World Trade Organisation (WTO, the body that sets rules for trade between countries) and regional trading blocs (groups of countries that trade on easier terms).
Growth of services and of remittances (money sent home by emigrants).
notes.tip: A Higher 30-mark question is expected on how a developing economy has adjusted to the global economy. Cover liberalisation, exports, foreign investment, debt and the IMF, trade blocs, and results and problems.

notes.h: India: colonial rule begins
notes.b: British control of India grew in two steps: first a trading company, then the Crown. Learn the dates, because the answer should name them.
points: The East India Company (a British trading company) was chartered on 31 December 1600 and first traded through trading posts.
The Battle of Plassey in 1757, won by Robert Clive, began Company rule in Bengal, so a trading firm became a ruler.
The Rebellion of 1857 led to the Government of India Act 1858, which transferred rule from the Company to the British Crown. This began direct British rule, known as the Raj.
India gained independence, so British rule ended, and was partitioned (divided into separate states) on 15 August 1947.
notes.tip: Higher answers are expected to name the country and give dates for the colonial period.

notes.h: India: deindustrialisation and cash crops
notes.b: Under British rule India moved from being a major manufacturer to a supplier of raw materials. This is deindustrialisation, the loss of an economy's industry.
points: India's large handloom textile industry, including Bengal's fine cottons and Dhaka (now in Bangladesh) muslin, was destroyed by cheap machine-made cloth from the cotton mills of Lancashire in north-west England.
Raw cotton was exported from India to Britain to feed those mills, so India sent out the raw material and bought back the cloth.

Economic historian Angus Maddison estimated India's share of world GDP (the value of all goods and services produced) at about a quarter around 1700 and about 4% by 1950. These are estimates, not exact figures.
Cash crops replaced food crops: cotton, jute, indigo (blue dye), tea from plantations in Assam from the 1830s–40s, and opium grown in India and exported to China.
Jute was processed in mills along the Hooghly near Calcutta, so the crop was processed near the port.
notes.tip: Give the Maddison figures as estimates. Remember that the destroyed industry and the cash crops are both part of the colonial economy an examiner expects.

notes.h: India: land revenue, famine and the drain of wealth
notes.b: British land taxes and the flow of money to Britain left Indian farmers poor and the country vulnerable to famine.
points: The Permanent Settlement of Bengal (1793, Lord Cornwallis) fixed land revenue (the tax paid on land) and collected it through zamindars, landlords who passed the tax burden on to peasants.
Heavy land taxes left the peasantry in debt and poverty, because the tax burden was passed on to them.
Famines (severe food shortages causing mass death) occurred under British rule: the Great Famine of 1876–78 and the Bengal famine of 1943.
The Bengal famine killed about 3 million people (estimates range from about 2 to 3 million). Grain was still exported while people starved.

The drain of wealth: revenue, profits and salaries were sent from India to Britain instead of being spent in India. Dadabhai Naoroji set out this argument in 'Poverty and Un-British Rule in India' (1901).
notes.tip: The Bengal famine toll is an estimate, so give it as about 3 million with the range of about 2 to 3 million.

notes.h: India: railways, ports and cities
notes.b: India's railways show how colonial infrastructure served the colonial power first.
points: The first passenger train ran from Bombay to Thane on 16 April 1853.
The railway network was built mainly to carry raw materials to the ports of Bombay and Calcutta and to move troops, so it served exports and control rather than Indian travellers.
Indians came to use the railways heavily, so they brought some benefit, although they were not built for Indian passengers' needs.
Ports and colonial cities grew, including Bombay (now Mumbai) and Calcutta (now Kolkata), because trade passed through them.
Calcutta was the capital of British India, until 1911, when the capital moved to Delhi.
notes.tip: Do not say India's railways were built for Indians. Say they were built mainly for exports and troops, though Indians came to use them heavily.

notes.h: India: political and social legacies
notes.b: British rule left India with lasting institutions, a language and a painful division, but also with a movement that ended it.
points: English is the language of government and business. It has since become an asset for India's IT industry. There is more on this in India in A Continental / Subcontinental Region.
India inherited a civil service, courts and a parliamentary system from British rule, so it did not start without institutions.
At independence, literacy was very low: about 18% in the 1951 census. Life expectancy was around 32 years.
Partition on 15 August 1947, the division of British India into separate states, displaced more than 10 million people, and hundreds of thousands were killed in the violence.
The Kashmir region has been disputed with Pakistan since 1947, so Partition left a lasting political conflict.

Mahatma Gandhi led a non-violent independence movement. Its methods included the boycott of British cloth, the promotion of swadeshi (buying Indian goods) and the spinning of khadi (hand-spun cloth), which struck at the cloth trade colonialism had built.
The Salt March of 1930 was a major act of resistance against British control, which is why it is a key example of resistance.
notes.tip: Cover the social legacy and the long-term effects: low literacy and life expectancy at independence, and the violence and displacement of Partition.

notes.h: India: state-led development after 1947
notes.b: After independence India's first adjustment was to let the state plan and own heavy industry, behind trade barriers.
points: The First Five-Year Plan (1951), under Jawaharlal Nehru, began a planned economy, in which the government sets targets for the economy in advance.
Import substitution (making at home what had been imported) behind high tariffs protected home industry from foreign competition.
The state built heavy industry, including steel plants at Bhilai, Rourkela and Durgapur.
The 'Licence Raj' meant that firms needed government licences to set up or expand, which restricted competition and investment.
Growth was slow, which is why it earned the nickname the 'Hindu rate of growth'.
notes.tip: For adjustment questions, name the stages in order and say what each did: state-led planning first, then the 1991 reforms.

notes.h: India: food self-sufficiency
notes.b: Food was a second adjustment, because the colonial economy had left India short of food.
points: The Green Revolution used high-yield seed varieties with fertiliser and irrigation to raise crop output.
Food-grain output rose from about 51 million tonnes in 1950–51 to about 330 million tonnes in 2022–23.
As a result India became self-sufficient in food, meaning it could feed itself without relying on imports.

notes.h: India: the 1991 crisis and liberalisation
notes.b: By 1991 state-led development had run into a financial crisis. India answered it by opening its economy, the third adjustment.
points: By 1991 foreign-exchange reserves (the foreign currency a country holds to pay for imports) had fallen to only enough for a few weeks of imports.
India pledged gold to raise loans and borrowed from the IMF (International Monetary Fund).

Reforms under Prime Minister P. V. Narasimha Rao and Finance Minister Manmohan Singh removed most licences, cut tariffs, welcomed foreign investment, privatised some state firms and devalued the rupee (lowered its value against other currencies).
India was a founding member of the WTO (World Trade Organisation) in 1995.
notes.tip: Examiners expect liberalisation, foreign investment, debt and the IMF in an answer on adjustment. Link the crisis to the reforms.

notes.h: India: results of opening up
notes.b: The 1991 reforms changed India's economy, so growth and the kind of work people did both shifted.
points: Growth became fast, and services (such as IT, as opposed to farming or manufacturing) now make up over half of GDP.
The IT and outsourcing industry (firms doing work for foreign companies) is based in Bengaluru, with firms such as TCS and Infosys.
Multinationals (firms operating in many countries) invest in India, encouraged by the Make in India programme (2014).
India is among the five largest economies in the world by GDP (early 2020s).
India is the world's largest recipient of remittances (money sent home by emigrants) (2020s).
notes.tip: Cover results and problems together, because an answer on adjustment is expected to include both.

notes.h: India: problems that remain
notes.b: Fast growth has not reached everyone. These problems are the other half of any answer on adjustment.
points: About nine-tenths of Indian workers are in the informal sector (2010s–2020s), without contracts, pensions or legal protection.
Agriculture still employs about 55% of workers (Census 2011), with low productivity, meaning each worker produces little.
Inequality exists between states: literacy was about 94% in Kerala and about 62% in Bihar (Census 2011).
Inequality also exists between rich and poor, so growth has not reached everyone.
India's HDI (Human Development Index, a measure combining income, health and education) is 0.644, 134th of 193 countries, in the medium category (Human Development Report 2023/24).
Infrastructure gaps and pollution remain serious problems, so growth is held back.
notes.tip: Give results and problems in the same answer. Include Kerala against Bihar for inequality between states.

notes.h: Brazil: Portuguese colonisation and export cycles
notes.b: Brazil was colonised by Portugal, not Spain, and its economy ran in cycles, each built on one export. Each cycle enriched Portugal and a small elite rather than the colony as a whole.
points: The Treaty of Tordesillas (1494) gave the east of South America to Portugal.
Pedro Álvares Cabral reached Brazil on 22 April 1500, which is why the Portuguese claim began there.
Brazil remained a Portuguese colony until independence on 7 September 1822, under Dom Pedro I.
Brazilwood, a red dye wood, gave the country its name, so the colony took its name from an export.
Sugar plantations in Pernambuco and Bahia in the North-East were the first major export.
Gold was mined in Minas Gerais ('general mines'), another export cycle.
Coffee was grown in São Paulo state in the 19th century, an export from the South-East.
The Amazon rubber boom centred on Manaus, from the late 19th century to about 1912, collapsed when plantations in British South-East Asia, grown from Brazilian seeds, undercut it.
notes.tip: Brazil was Portuguese, not Spanish, and its language is Portuguese. Name the cycles in order and say who gained from each.

notes.h: Brazil: slavery, indigenous peoples and land
notes.b: Colonial Brazil depended on forced labour, took land from its first peoples and concentrated land in few hands. All three still shape inequality today.
points: About 4 to 5 million enslaved Africans were taken to Brazil, more than to any other country in the Americas. They worked on plantations and in mines. This is an estimate.
Slavery was abolished by the Lei Áurea (Golden Law) on 13 May 1888. Brazil was the last country in the Americas to abolish it.
The legacy of slavery includes racial inequality: Afro-Brazilians are over-represented among the poor and in favelas (poor urban neighbourhoods).
Indigenous peoples were killed by disease, war and enslavement, and pushed off their land, so they are now a small minority.
Census 2022 counted about 1.7 million indigenous people, under 1% of Brazil's population of about 203 million.
Huge estates (latifundia), originating in Portuguese land grants, are owned by a few families, while millions of rural workers are landless.
Brazil has one of the most unequal patterns of land ownership in the world, which means many rural workers have no land.
The MST (Landless Workers' Movement), founded in 1984, campaigns for land reform (a fairer sharing of land). Conflict over land in the Amazon continues.
notes.tip: Brazil's slavery figures are estimates, so give them as about 4 to 5 million.

notes.h: Brazil: regional inequality and primary exports
notes.b: Because each export cycle sat in one region, its decline left that region poor, and the country stayed tied to exporting raw materials.
points: When sugar declined, the North-East was left poor.
Wealth and industry shifted to the South-East: São Paulo (Brazil's largest city and industrial centre), Rio de Janeiro and Minas Gerais.
Migrants moved from the North-East to the South-East cities and their favelas, looking for work.
SUDENE, the agency for developing the North-East, was set up in 1959.
The colonial pattern of exporting raw materials continued after independence, with coffee dominating exports for much of that period. This left Brazil exposed to changes in world prices.
notes.tip: Examiners expect long-term effects on the economy today. The North-East against the South-East is a clear example.

notes.h: Brazil: import substitution and the Brazilian miracle
notes.b: From the 1930s Brazil's first adjustment was state-led industrialisation behind trade barriers, replacing imports with goods made at home.
points: Getúlio Vargas was president from 1930 to 1945 and from 1951 to 1954. His government promoted state-led industrialisation, meaning the state drove it.
Petrobras, the state oil company, was founded in 1953, so the state controlled a key industry.
President Juscelino Kubitschek (1956–61) promised 'fifty years of progress in five' and built a car industry.
The new capital, Brasília, was inaugurated on 21 April 1960 to open up the interior, since development had been concentrated on the coast.
The Manaus Free Trade Zone (an area with tax benefits for firms) was created in 1967.
The 'Brazilian miracle', so called because of very fast growth, about 1968–73, took place under military rule (1964–85).

notes.h: Brazil: heavy borrowing, debt and stabilisation
notes.b: Growth was paid for with foreign loans, and the debt later caused a crisis that forced a change of course.
points: Brazil borrowed heavily from foreign lenders, which made it exposed when it could not repay.
The 1980s debt crisis, known as the 'lost decade', brought hyperinflation (prices rising extremely fast) and IMF programmes.
The Plano Real (1994) ended hyperinflation, which means prices became stable again, and introduced the real as the currency.
notes.tip: For adjustment questions, include debt and the IMF as a stage, and say what ended the crisis.

notes.h: Brazil: opening up and commodity exports
notes.b: From the 1990s Brazil opened its economy to trade and investment, and a boom in commodities (raw materials traded in bulk) followed, with China as the main buyer.
points: The iron-ore miner Vale (formerly Companhia Vale do Rio Doce) was privatised (sold to private owners) in 1997. Its Carajás mines are in Pará.
Mercosur, the trade bloc of Argentina, Paraguay, Uruguay and Brazil, was founded in 1991 by the Treaty of Asunción.
A commodity export boom sent soya, iron ore, oil, beef and coffee abroad, especially to China.
China has been Brazil's largest trading partner since 2009, because it buys so many of these commodities.
Brazil is the world's largest producer and exporter of soya beans and the largest producer of coffee (2020s).
Brazil is a member of BRICS, a group of large emerging economies. The BRIC term was coined in 2001 by Jim O'Neill of Goldman Sachs, and the first BRIC summit was held in 2009.
Embraer, the aircraft maker in São José dos Campos (São Paulo state), is a high-tech export, which shows exports beyond raw materials.
notes.tip: Cover trade blocs, exports and privatisation as stages of adjustment.

notes.h: Brazil: poverty reduction and its limits
notes.b: Brazil cut hunger and poverty, but adjustment had costs. Inequality, deforestation and dependence on commodity prices remain.
points: Bolsa Família, launched in 2003 under President Lula da Silva, gives cash to poor families on condition that children attend school and are vaccinated.
Brazil left the UN (FAO) World Hunger Map in 2014, which shows that Bolsa Família and growth cut hunger.
Brazil's HDI (a measure combining income, health and education) is about 0.76, in the high category (Human Development Report 2023/24).
Brazil is among the most unequal countries in the world by the Gini coefficient (a measure of how unequally income is shared).
Cattle ranching is the largest driver of Amazon deforestation, with soya expansion also contributing.
Commodity dependence brought a recession in 2015–16, when commodity prices fell.
The North-East is still the poorest region of Brazil, so the colonial regional gap has lasted.
The WTO ruled in Brazil's favour against US cotton subsidies (government payments to farmers) in 2004–05. There is more on this in Global issues and a justice perspective.
notes.tip: Examiners expect results and problems. Pair each gain, such as Bolsa Família, with a limit, such as inequality or price dependence.

notes.h: Sudan: Egyptian and Mahdist rule, then British control
notes.b: Sudan here means Sudan before 2011, including today's South Sudan. It was ruled by Egypt, then by a Mahdist state, and then in practice by Britain.
points: Egyptian conquest began in 1821, so Sudan was first ruled from Egypt.
The Mahdist state (1885–98) was led by Muhammad Ahmad, 'the Mahdi'. Its forces took Khartoum in 1885 and killed General Gordon.
British forces under Kitchener defeated the Mahdists at the Battle of Omdurman on 2 September 1898.
The Anglo-Egyptian Condominium (1899–1956), a joint-rule arrangement, was in practice British rule.
Sudan became independent on 1 January 1956. Its capital, Khartoum, lies at the confluence (meeting point) of the Blue and White Niles.
notes.tip: Sudan's capital is Khartoum. South Sudan's is Juba.

notes.h: Sudan: the Gezira Scheme and cotton
notes.b: The Gezira Scheme shows a colonial economy built for the colonial power. It turned Sudan into a supplier of one crop.
points: The Gezira Scheme is an irrigation scheme between the Blue and White Niles, south of Khartoum.
The Sennar Dam on the Blue Nile was completed in 1925 to water the scheme, so cotton could grow on dry land. Do not confuse it with the Aswan Dam, which is in Egypt.
The scheme covers nearly 900,000 hectares and is one of the world's largest irrigation schemes.
It grew long-staple cotton for the Lancashire mills, not for Sudan's own industry.
Tenant farmers (farmers who rent their land) grew the cotton under strict control.
Cotton became Sudan's main export, so the economy depended on one crop and its world price.
Investment was concentrated in the Nile valley around Khartoum and Gezira. The south, Darfur and other peripheral regions (areas far from the centre) were neglected.
notes.tip: The Gezira cotton was for Lancashire mills, not for Sudan's own industry. Say that the economy depended on one crop and its world price.

notes.h: Sudan: the Southern Policy and borders
notes.b: Britain ran Sudan as two regions and then joined them. This is the root of Sudan's civil wars.
points: From the 1920s Britain ran the Arab and Muslim north and the African, largely Christian and animist (following traditional spiritual beliefs) south as separate regions.
The Closed District Ordinance (1922) restricted northerners' entry to the south, so the two regions were kept apart.
English and Christian missions worked in the south, while Arabic was used in the north, so the two regions grew apart.
The regions were joined into one state at independence, and power went to a northern elite.
Colonial boundaries enclosed many ethnic, language and religious groups within one state. This laid the basis for civil war.
notes.tip: Examiners expect borders and political legacy. Link the colonial borders to the civil wars.

notes.h: Sudan: civil wars and the separation of South Sudan
notes.b: The colonial legacy of division led to decades of war and finally to the separation of the south.
points: The first civil war (1955–72) ended with the Addis Ababa Agreement (1972).
The second civil war (1983–2005) killed about 2 million people. It ended with the Comprehensive Peace Agreement in January 2005.
The Darfur conflict began in 2003. The UN estimated about 300,000 deaths, and the International Criminal Court issued an arrest warrant for President al-Bashir in 2009.
A referendum (a public vote on one question) in January 2011 gave about 99% support for independence. South Sudan became independent on 9 July 2011, with its capital at Juba.
Sudan here means Sudan before 2011, which included today's South Sudan.

notes.h: Sudan: cotton, borrowing and famine after independence
notes.b: Independence did not change the economy's basic shape. Sudan stayed tied to cotton and slid into debt.
points: Sudan remained dependent on Gezira cotton after independence, so it was still exposed to the world price.
Governments attempted state-led development, so the state tried to drive growth.
Heavy borrowing led to debt, so IMF programmes followed.
A famine caused by drought and war struck the country.
notes.tip: For adjustment questions, include debt and the IMF.

notes.h: Sudan: oil and the loss of South Sudan
notes.b: Oil brought fast growth from 1999, but most of it lay in the south, so Sudan lost much of it when the south separated.
points: Oil exports began in 1999 through a pipeline to Port Sudan on the Red Sea.
The main buyers and investors were Chinese state oil firms, with Malaysian and Indian firms also involved. China was the main buyer.
Oil became the main export, and GDP grew fast in the 2000s.
Most oil lay in the south. South Sudan's independence in 2011 took about three-quarters of Sudan's oil production.
The loss of oil caused an economic crisis, with inflation (rising prices) and protests.
South Sudan is landlocked, so it still exports its oil through Sudan's pipeline.
notes.tip: Say that most oil lay in the south, so independence in 2011 removed about three-quarters of production and caused the crisis.

notes.h: Sudan: isolation, debt and other exports
notes.b: Sanctions and debt cut Sudan off from the global economy, while its other exports remained raw materials.
points: The United States listed Sudan as a 'state sponsor of terrorism' from 1993 to 2020, when the listing was removed in December 2020. The sanctions (penalties restricting trade and finance) cut Sudan off from Western banks and investment.
Sudan has one of the world's largest debt burdens. It reached the HIPC decision point in 2021, a step in a debt-relief process for heavily indebted poor countries.
Sudan is the world's largest producer of gum arabic, from acacia trees, which is used in food and drinks.
Other exports include gold, livestock and sesame, so the economy still relies on primary products.

notes.h: Sudan: political turmoil and the present
notes.b: Political instability has now reversed Sudan's development.
points: President Omar al-Bashir was in power from 1989 to 2019 and was removed in April 2019 after mass protests.
A military coup took place in October 2021, so the 2019 change did not bring stable civilian rule.
Since 15 April 2023 the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) have been at war.
More than 10 million people had been displaced (forced to leave their homes) by 2024, the largest displacement crisis in the world.
Famine was confirmed in Zamzam camp, North Darfur, in August 2024.
Development has gone into reverse because of war and displacement, and Sudan is in the low human development category.
notes.tip: Do not give a death toll for the 2023 war, because estimates vary widely.

keyTerms.definition: The control of one territory and its people by a foreign power, which rules it, settles it and/or exploits its resources for the colonising country.
A crop grown for sale abroad rather than to feed the people who grow it.
Dependence on a single crop or product for a country's export earnings.
The decline of a country's manufacturing, such as India's handloom textiles, after competition from cheaper imports.
The transfer of revenue, profits and salaries from a colony to the colonising country.
A landlord who collected land revenue for the British in Bengal under the Permanent Settlement.
The system after independence in which firms needed government licences to set up or expand.
A strategy of protecting new home industries from foreign competition with tariffs, so that goods once imported are made at home.
Conditions attached to IMF and World Bank loans, such as cutting government spending, privatising, opening to trade and devaluing the currency.
Opening an economy to trade and foreign investment, and reducing state control.
A large irrigation scheme in Sudan, watered by the Sennar Dam, that grew cotton for the Lancashire mills.
British policy from the 1920s of running northern and southern Sudan as separate regions, which laid the basis for civil war.

factCards.definition: Colonies sent cheap raw materials (cotton, sugar, rubber, minerals) to the colonial power and bought its manufactured goods; competing local industries were destroyed; plantations and mines used forced or slave labour; export cash crops replaced food crops.

factCards.term: Colonialism: four lasting political and social legacies
factCards.definition: Artificial borders split some ethnic groups and grouped rivals together; 'divide and rule' and weak institutions handed over at independence led to conflict and coups; education only for a small elite; land owned by a few.

factCards.definition: The Treaty of Tordesillas (1494) gave the east of South America to Portugal; Pedro Álvares Cabral reached Brazil on 22 April 1500; independence came on 7 September 1822 under Dom Pedro I.

factCards.term: Brazil: the colonial export cycles in order
factCards.definition: Brazilwood, a red dye wood (the country's name); sugar in Pernambuco and Bahia (North-East); gold in Minas Gerais; coffee in São Paulo state (19th century); rubber at Manaus until about 1912, undercut by plantations in British South-East Asia.

factCards.term: Brazil: slavery and its legacy
factCards.definition: About 4 to 5 million enslaved Africans were taken to Brazil, more than any other country in the Americas. The Lei Áurea (Golden Law) ended slavery on 13 May 1888, the last in the Americas. Afro-Brazilians are over-represented among the poor and in favelas.

factCards.term: Brazil: effects of colonisation on indigenous people and land
factCards.definition: Indigenous peoples were killed by disease, war and enslavement and lost their land: about 1.7 million today, under 1% of the population (Census 2022). Latifundia from Portuguese land grants left land with a few families; the MST (1984) campaigns for land.

factCards.term: Brazil: how colonialism left regional inequality
factCards.definition: Sugar's decline left the North-East poor; wealth and industry moved to the South-East (São Paulo, Rio de Janeiro, Minas Gerais), drawing migrants to favelas. SUDENE (1959) was set up to develop the North-East. Coffee dominated exports after independence.

factCards.term: Brazil: import substitution and the Brazilian miracle
factCards.definition: Getúlio Vargas (1930–45, 1951–54) began state-led industry; Petrobras, 1953; Juscelino Kubitschek (1956–61): fifty years of progress in five, a car industry, Brasília (inaugurated 21 April 1960); the Brazilian miracle, about 1968–73, under military rule.

factCards.term: Brazil: debt crisis and stabilisation
factCards.definition: Heavy foreign borrowing led to the 1980s debt crisis, the lost decade, with hyperinflation and IMF programmes. The Plano Real (1994) ended hyperinflation and introduced the real as the currency.

factCards.term: Brazil: privatisation and trade blocs when opening up
factCards.definition: Vale, the iron-ore miner with Carajás mines in Pará, was privatised in 1997. Mercosur was founded in 1991 by the Treaty of Asunción with Argentina, Paraguay and Uruguay. Brazil is in BRICS: Jim O'Neill of Goldman Sachs coined BRIC in 2001; first summit 2009.

factCards.term: Brazil: commodity boom and a high-tech export
factCards.definition: Soya, iron ore, oil, beef and coffee, especially to China, Brazil's largest trading partner since 2009. Brazil is the world's largest producer and exporter of soya beans and largest coffee producer (2020s). Embraer (São José dos Campos) exports aircraft.

factCards.term: Brazil: Bolsa Família and the limits of poverty reduction
factCards.definition: Bolsa Família (2003, President Lula da Silva) pays poor families if children attend school and are vaccinated; Brazil left the FAO World Hunger Map in 2014. But inequality is among the world's highest by the Gini coefficient; HDI about 0.76 (2023/24 report).

factCards.term: Brazil: four costs of adjusting to the global economy
factCards.definition: Amazon deforestation, driven mainly by cattle ranching and also soya; dependence on commodity prices, bringing recession in 2015–16 when prices fell; favelas; the North-East still the poorest region.

factCards.term: Sudan: five dates in its colonial history
factCards.definition: Egyptian conquest 1821; Mahdist state 1885–98 (the Mahdi's forces took Khartoum and killed General Gordon in 1885); Battle of Omdurman, 2 September 1898 (Kitchener); Anglo-Egyptian Condominium 1899–1956, in practice British rule; independence 1 January 1956.

factCards.term: Gezira Scheme: location, size, purpose and effect
factCards.definition: Between the Blue and White Niles south of Khartoum, watered by the Sennar Dam on the Blue Nile (1925); nearly 900,000 hectares. Tenant farmers grew long-staple cotton for Lancashire mills under strict control, so Sudan depended on one crop's world price.

factCards.term: Sudan: how British rule divided the country
factCards.definition: Investment went to the Nile valley around Khartoum and Gezira; the south and Darfur were neglected. The Southern Policy (1920s) and Closed District Ordinance (1922) kept the Arab, Muslim north and the African, largely Christian and animist south apart; power then went to a northern elite.

factCards.term: Sudan: the two civil wars and South Sudan's independence
factCards.definition: First civil war 1955–72, ended by the Addis Ababa Agreement; second 1983–2005, about 2 million deaths, ended by the Comprehensive Peace Agreement (January 2005). About 99% voted for independence in January 2011; South Sudan became independent on 9 July 2011.

factCards.term: Darfur conflict: start date and two key facts
factCards.definition: It began in 2003. The UN estimated about 300,000 deaths, and the International Criminal Court issued an arrest warrant for President al-Bashir in 2009.

factCards.term: Sudan after independence: four features of its economy before oil
factCards.definition: Continued dependence on Gezira cotton; state-led development attempts; heavy borrowing leading to debt and IMF programmes; famine in the 1980s caused by drought and war.

factCards.term: Sudan's oil: when exports began and why the boom ended
factCards.definition: Exports began in 1999 by pipeline to Port Sudan, with China the main buyer and investor; GDP grew fast in the 2000s. Most oil lay in the south, so South Sudan's independence in 2011 took about three-quarters of output, causing inflation and protests.

factCards.term: Sudan: isolation, debt and other primary exports
factCards.definition: US listing as a state sponsor of terrorism (1993–2020) cut it off from Western banks and investment; one of the world's largest debt burdens, reaching the HIPC decision point in 2021. Exports: gum arabic (world's largest producer), gold, livestock, sesame.

factCards.term: Sudan today: political turmoil since 2019
factCards.definition: Omar al-Bashir (in power 1989–2019) was removed in April 2019 after mass protests; military coup October 2021; war between the SAF and RSF since 15 April 2023; more than 10 million displaced (2024); famine confirmed in Zamzam camp, North Darfur, August 2024.

questions.prompt: Examine the impact of colonialism on a developing economy that you have studied.
questions.model: India under British rule was a clear example of colonialism's impact. The East India Company was chartered on 31 December 1600, and after the Battle of Plassey in 1757 it ruled Bengal. The Rebellion of 1857 led to direct British rule under the Crown from 1858. Colonial economic policy destroyed India's handloom textile industry, as cheap machine-made cloth from the Lancashire mills displaced Bengal's fine cottons and Dhaka muslin, while raw cotton was exported to Britain. India's share of world GDP fell from about a quarter around 1700 to about 4% by 1950, according to Maddison's estimates. Cash crops such as cotton, jute, indigo, tea from Assam and opium for China replaced food crops, leaving farmers exposed to shortages. The Permanent Settlement of 1793 fixed land revenue through zamindars, which kept the peasantry in debt, and famines occurred, including the Bengal famine of 1943 which killed about 3 million people, while grain was still exported. Revenue and profits were drained to Britain, an argument Dadabhai Naoroji made in 1901. Railways were built mainly to carry raw materials to Bombay and Calcutta and to move troops, so they did not link regions for Indian needs. Ports and colonial cities such as Bombay and Calcutta grew while the interior remained underdeveloped. Social and political legacies included very low literacy, about 18% in 1951, and a life expectancy of about 32 years at independence. Partition in 1947 displaced more than 10 million people, and the Kashmir dispute continues. The English language, a civil service and a parliamentary system remained after independence. Long-term effects include the regional inequality between states that still exists today, and a HDI of 0.644 that remains in the medium category.

questions.prompt: Describe and explain how a developing economy that you have studied has adjusted to a global economy.
questions.model: Brazil shows how a developing economy adjusted in stages. Its economy was built on export cycles, including brazilwood, sugar, gold, coffee and the Amazon rubber boom centred on Manaus, which enriched Portugal and a small elite, and after independence in 1822 coffee dominated exports. Its adjustment began with import substitution under Getúlio Vargas, who created the state oil company Petrobras in 1953, and Juscelino Kubitschek, whose Brasília opened the interior in 1960. The Manaus Free Trade Zone was created in 1967, and the Brazilian miracle of fast growth took place under military rule about 1968–73. Heavy borrowing led to the 1980s debt crisis, the lost decade, with hyperinflation and IMF programmes, until the Plano Real of 1994 ended hyperinflation. Opening up included privatising Vale in 1997, joining the Mercosur trade bloc in 1991, and becoming a BRICS member. A commodity boom sent soya, iron ore, oil, beef and coffee abroad, and China has been Brazil's largest trading partner since 2009. Brazil is the largest producer of soya beans and coffee. Embraer aircraft are a high-tech export. Poverty was reduced by Bolsa Família, launched in 2003, which pays families on condition that children attend school and are vaccinated, and Brazil left the UN World Hunger Map in 2014. Problems remain: Brazil is among the most unequal countries in the world, and its HDI of about 0.76 is high but inequality persists. Costs include Amazon deforestation driven by cattle ranching and soya, and recession in 2015–16 when commodity prices fell. The North-East is still the poorest region.

questions.prompt: Name one developing economy that was colonised. Describe and explain the effects of colonialism on this economy.
questions.model: Sudan, before 2011 including today's South Sudan, was colonised by Egypt from 1821 and then ruled by Britain. After the Mahdist state was defeated at the Battle of Omdurman on 2 September 1898, the Anglo-Egyptian Condominium (1899–1956) was in practice British rule until independence on 1 January 1956. The Gezira Scheme, watered by the Sennar Dam completed in 1925, grew long-staple cotton for the Lancashire mills, so Sudan's economy depended on one crop and its world price. Tenant farmers grew the cotton under strict control. Investment was concentrated in the Nile valley around Khartoum and Gezira, and the south and Darfur were neglected. From the 1920s the Southern Policy ran the north and south as separate regions, with English and Christian missions in the south and Arabic in the north, and the regions were joined at independence with power going to a northern elite. Colonial boundaries enclosed many ethnic, language and religious groups. This led to civil wars: the first from 1955 to 1972, and the second from 1983 to 2005, which killed about 2 million people. The Darfur conflict began in 2003. Oil exports began in 1999 through a pipeline to Port Sudan, mainly for China, but most oil lay in the south, and South Sudan's independence in 2011 took about three-quarters of production, causing an economic crisis with inflation and protests.
